paras: The attempted lynching of William Medley took place in the Bear Quarter section of Norfolk County, Virginia, on about February 10, 1882, when residents tried to lynch a Black man accused of assaulting a five-year-old girl. Constable David Sykes got him to jail, and a Norfolk dispatch noted that the angry residents included both whites and Black people. Medley was later tried in the county court and sentenced to twenty years in the penitentiary.

Medley, described as "a negro," was accused of a "brutal assault" on the five-year-old daughter of John Weatherfield, called "a respectable farmer of that section." The dispatch said the child had been "terribly injured."

On Thursday, February 9, Medley was tried before Justice Warren at Bear Quarter and committed to jail. Constable David Sykes took him to the county jail, where a Richmond Dispatch telegram said he was lodged on the morning of February 10. According to the Norfolk dispatch, he "was with difficulty saved from being lynched by the infuriated residents of Bear Quarter, both whites and blacks." The dispatch gives no number for the crowd and does not say where or how the residents tried to reach him.

No arrest of anyone in the crowd appears in the coverage. In late March, Medley was "on trial for his life" in the Norfolk County Court, and the Alexandria Gazette reported that the jury had been hung for two days, with four jurors for hanging and eight for eighteen years in the penitentiary. On June 22 he was convicted of having "attempted to outrage a child in Pleasant Grove district" and sentenced to twenty years in the penitentiary.

The near-lynching was known outside Norfolk through a single dispatch headed "A Shocking Crime," which ran in the Alexandria Gazette on February 11 and in a Delaware paper, The Daily Gazette, on February 13. The two copies differ in dateline and spelling, one dated February 11 with "Medley" and "Bar Quarter," the other dated February 10 with "Medly." The Richmond Dispatch carried its own Norfolk telegram under the headline "A Fiendish Crime," reporting the jailing and the charge but not the mob.

All three February reports put the alleged crime in the headline and treated the threatened lynching, where they mentioned it at all, in a closing sentence without comment. The trial and sentence ran as short items in the Alexandria Gazette and the Richmond Dispatch, the latter under the headline "Twenty Years in the Penitentiary."

The February reports describe a completed "brutal assault" or "terrible outrage," while the June conviction reports describe an attempt to "outrage" a child. The February reports place the crime at Bear Quarter, and the June reports in Pleasant Grove district, which may describe the same area at different scales.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of William Medley
bases: Residents of Bear Quarter tried to lynch a jailed Black man accused of assaulting a child and he was 'with difficulty saved' by the constable, an attempted lynching with no death (A1, A3).
No one was killed: Medley was saved from the 'infuriated residents' and later tried and sentenced in court (A1, A3, A5); the episode is an attempted lynching, not a completed one.

The near-lynching appears only in one Norfolk dispatch carried by two papers (A1, A3); a separate Norfolk telegram confirms the arrest and accusation but says nothing of a mob (A2), and the later court reports confirm the prosecution (A4, A5, A6).

accounts.label: Norfolk wire dispatch ('A Shocking Crime')
accounts.gist: Medley was tried, committed to jail, and saved with difficulty from lynching by white and Black residents of Bear Quarter.

accounts.label: Richmond Dispatch special telegram
accounts.gist: Medley was lodged in the county jail on the morning of February 10 for the outrage; no mob is mentioned.

accounts.label: Court reports
accounts.gist: A first jury hung over hanging versus prison; in June he was convicted of attempting to outrage a child and given twenty years.

framing.detail: The 'A Shocking Crime' dispatch calls the assault 'brutal', the girl 'terribly injured' and the residents 'infuriated', reporting the near-lynching without comment.
The Richmond Dispatch headlined its telegram 'A Fiendish Crime' and reported only the jailing and the accusation.
The trial and sentence ran as brief news items, the June one in the Alexandria Gazette's 'Virginia News' column.

conflicts.note: A2 is a direct special telegram and A3 carries the same dispatch as A1 dated Feb. 10, so February 10 is better supported; A1's dateline appears to be re-dated.
Not necessarily contradictory: the June reports name a district, the February ones a neighborhood.
The conviction reports describe an attempt rather than a completed outrage.

record_check.dossier: William Medley in four of five reports; 'Medly' only in A3.
February 9 was the hearing before Justice Warren; the jailing and lynching threat were February 10.
The dispatch reports only that he was 'with difficulty saved from being lynched'; no siege of a jail is described.
Residents of Bear Quarter, 'both whites and blacks'.
Six white articles in three papers, including the March trial and the June conviction and twenty-year sentence.

info: Medley was tried before Justice Warren on Thursday, February 9, 1882, and lodged in the county jail on the morning of February 10; the lynching threat came as he was taken to jail.
Bear Quarter ('Bar Quarter', 'Bearquarter section'), Norfolk county; the conviction reports place the alleged crime in Pleasant Grove district.
William Medley (also 'Medly'), described as 'a negro'; not harmed.
Accused of a 'brutal assault' ('terrible outrage') on a five-year-old girl, daughter of farmer John Weatherfield; convicted in June of having 'attempted to outrage' a child.
'The infuriated residents of Bear Quarter, both whites and blacks.'
Convicted June 22, 1882, and sentenced to twenty years in the penitentiary.
